subjective.question: Differentiate between traditional marketing and Customer Relationship Management (CRM).
subjective.answer: Traditional marketing focuses on individual transactions and on gaining new and more customers, not on retaining existing ones. CRM, by contrast, focuses on continuous multiple transactions rather than individual ones, and on customers and the entire functions connected with value creation and delivery in the organization. CRM attracts, maintains and enhances relationships, using psychology rather than economic inducements to attract and retain customers. It is the acquisition of customers by understanding and fulfilling their requirements more than expectations, and includes the methodologies, strategies and capabilities that help an enterprise organize and manage customer relationships.

subjective.question: State the general purpose of CRM and its major areas of focus.
subjective.answer: The general purpose of CRM is to enable organizations to better manage their customers through reliable systems and methods, so they can service existing customers more emphatically and forcefully, and to develop processes and procedures for interacting with customers under a framework of systems and regulations. Its major focus areas are generation and servicing of more loyal customers, expansion of the customer base, reduction of advertising costs, increase in profitable customers, ease in introducing new products, personal information gathering and processing, and self-service. CRM thus aims at retention after acquisition.

subjective.question: Why do organizations lose their customers? Explain the main reasons.
subjective.answer: Organizations lose customers for price-related, product-related, service-related, benefit-related, competitor and personal reasons. Price is one of the most important reasons worldwide, as customers are attracted by discounts, special prices and rebates, as seen with mobile phone companies offering lower call rates. Product-related reasons arise when another product offers better quality or extra benefits. Service and benefit reasons also cause switching, while competitors may offer a better quality product or service package. Personal reasons such as contacts, group decisions or prestige also carry considerable weight in switching.

subjective.question: On what factors do strategies for building relationship management differ from one organization to another?
subjective.answer: Relationship-building strategies differ according to the nature of the business, including its extent and geographical coverage; the size of market share, which affects personalized service and complaint handling; the nature of the product, whether essential-for-life, comfort, luxury, life-saving or image-making; the volume of sales; geographic concentration of sales; socio-economic status, as urban areas usually have stronger buying power than rural areas; the lifestyle of people; and the strength of competitors, whose weak areas may be targeted more easily than their strongholds.

subjective.question: How can a good CRM program improve customer service by facilitating communication?
subjective.answer: A good CRM program improves service by providing product information, product use information and technical assistance on websites accessible 24 hours a day, 7 days a week; identifying how each customer defines quality and designing a service strategy for each; providing a fast mechanism for follow-up sales calls; tracking all points of contact in an integrated way; identifying potential problems quickly before they occur; providing user-friendly complaint registration and fast complaint handling; correcting service deficiencies quickly; using internet cookies to personalize offerings; and managing maintenance, repair and ongoing support efficiently.

subjective.question: Define customer service and explain the two key ideas in its definition.
subjective.answer: Customer service is the provision of labour and other resources for the purpose of increasing the value that buyers receive from their purchases and from the processes leading up to the purchase. All departments, not only marketing and sales, must orient their work towards customer happiness, because labour across purchasing, manufacturing and distribution serves the customer. Value is not only the product itself: a buyer of an air conditioner also receives installation, ease of maintenance, spare parts, convenience, warranty and backup services, and considers this whole service package before patronizing a seller.

subjective.question: How does customer service provide a strategic advantage to a company?
subjective.answer: Customer service can be a preserved difference that lets a company outperform rivals, because it is very difficult to control and therefore difficult to imitate. Its level may vary greatly between two providers in the same organization, and from one moment to another even with the same provider, and this variability is compounded in multi-unit operations. Consistent delivery of superior service requires careful design and execution of a whole system involving people, capital, technology and processes. Companies that manage this system stand out and are sought out, which is the foundation of their sustainable competitive advantage.

subjective.question: Trace the history of customer service from the Craftsman Economy to the 1990s.
subjective.answer: In the Craftsman Economy of the 1800s, manufacturers produced arts and crafts to individual orders, meeting customers one-to-one, so service was highly personalized. Mass production in the early 20th century and the explosion in demand after World War II increased suppliers' power at consumers' expense and reduced the importance of customer service, when demand exceeded supply. In the 1970s, international competition, first from Japan, then Korea, China and other developing economies, shifted the balance and producers improved quality and service. The 1990s boom again increased supplier power, making them more selective about customers and service levels.

subjective.question: What does a customer want? Describe the four categories given in the handout.
subjective.answer: Customers want four things. Good People who are friendly, helpful, courteous, empathetic, knowledgeable, accurate, thorough, resourceful, empowered, efficient, trustworthy and reliable. A Good Offering with good selection and quality, items in stock, clear descriptions and pricing, competitive prices and financing options. Convenience through convenient locations, long hours, available help, fast service and checkout, delivery, installation, phone/web support and hassle-free returns. And a Good Environment that is clean, organized, safe and low pressure, with an energy level appropriate to the clientele. Together these give a trouble-free procurement experience.

subjective.question: State and explain the three requirements in complaint handling.
subjective.answer: First, complaints should be positively encouraged, because the main problem lies with the many customers who do not complain and instead switch to another supplier. Second, all complaints should be carefully handled by painstakingly controlled and monitored procedures, and be seen to be well handled by both the complainant and the organization's staff. Third, and most importantly, the complaint should be fully investigated and the cause remedied, because complaints are only symptoms and the disease needs to be cured. It is far better to assume that one complaint is too many than to wait until complaints reach a damaging level.

subjective.question: Explain why implementing CRM requires a holistic approach, and describe the three aspects it includes.
subjective.answer: A successful CRM strategy cannot be implemented by simply installing and integrating a software package; the main misconception is that CRM is only software, whereas it is a whole business strategy oriented on customer needs. A holistic approach is needed, with close and careful implementation and monitoring by the entire management, including top management. It includes three aspects: training of employees at all levels, periodically and kept updated, covering technical use of software and IT applications plus attitude and behavioural training towards customers; modification of business processes based on customers' needs; and adoption of relevant IT systems, including software and hardware, or IT services that enable the company to follow its CRM strategy.

subjective.question: Describe what a good CRM program needs to do.
subjective.answer: A good CRM program needs to identify each customer's success factor, meaning the strength in the customer's business, such as a good financial system, speed of work or quality of product, and always be mindful of it. It should create a customer-based culture in which all work, efforts and objectives focus on customers, and adopt customer-based measures so strategies and policies provide maximum convenience and comfort, even down to product packing. It should develop an end-to-end process to serve customers, recommend what to tell a customer with a complaint under a uniform policy, and track all aspects of selling to customers and prospects as well as customer support.

subjective.question: What is operational CRM? Describe its three general areas of business.
subjective.answer: Operational CRM means supporting the 'front office' business processes, which include customer contact in sales, marketing and service. It delivers personalised and efficient marketing, sales and service, enables a 360-degree view of the customer during interaction, and gives sales and service staff the complete history of customer interactions. Its three general areas are: Sales Force Automation, which automates lead and account management, contact management, forecasting and sales administration, with mobile synchronisation and integrated product configuration as key infrastructure; Customer Service and Support, which automates service requests, complaints and returns and has evolved into the customer interaction centre using computer telephony integration; and Enterprise Marketing Automation, which provides information about competitors, industry trends and the macro environment.

subjective.question: Explain analytical CRM, including the types of campaigns directed towards customers.
subjective.answer: In analytical CRM, data gathered within operational CRM and from other sources are analysed to segment customers or to identify potential to enhance the client relationship. Customer analysis typically leads to targeted campaigns to increase the share of the customer's wallet. Campaigns directed towards customers include acquisition, through cross-sell and up-sell; retention, retaining customers who leave due to maturity or attrition; information, providing timely and regular information to customers; and modification, altering details of the transactional nature of the customer's relationship. The analysis itself may relate to campaign management, customer segmentation, customer satisfaction measurement, sales coverage optimisation, fraud detection, financial forecasts, pricing optimisation, product development and risk assessment.

subjective.question: What is collaborative CRM and what benefits does it provide?
subjective.answer: Collaborative CRM facilitates interactions with customers through all channels, including personal contact, letter, fax, phone, web and e-mail, and supports the co-ordination of employee teams and channels. It is a solution that brings people, processes and data together so companies can better serve and retain their customers; the data and activities may be structured, unstructured, conversational and transactional in nature. Its benefits are that it enables efficient, productive customer interactions across all communications channels, enables web collaboration to reduce customer service costs, integrates call centres enabling multi-channel personal customer interaction, and integrates the view of the customer while interacting at the transaction level.

subjective.question: How do CRM programs improve customer relationships?
subjective.answer: CRM technology can track customer interests, needs and buying habits as they progress through their life cycles, and tailor the marketing effort accordingly, so customers get exactly what they want as they change. It can also track customer product use as the product progresses through its life cycle and tailor the service strategy accordingly. In industrial markets it can micro-segment the buying centre and help coordinate members' conflicting purchase criteria. Improvements in customer service can ensure repeat purchases, increase loyalty, decrease customer turnover and marketing costs, and increase sales revenue and profit margins. Repeat purchase comes from customer satisfaction, which comes from a deeper understanding of each customer rather than a 'one size fits all' approach.

subjective.question: Describe the technical functionality that characterises a CRM solution.
subjective.answer: A CRM solution is characterised by several technical functions. Scalability is the ability to be used on a large scale and to be reliably expanded to whatever scale is necessary. Multiple communication channels means the ability to interface with users via many different devices, such as phone, WAP and internet. Workflow is the ability to trigger a process in the back office system, for example an e-mail response. Assignment is the ability to assign requests, such as service requests and sales opportunities, to a person or group. The database provides centralised storage, in a data warehouse, of all information relevant to customer interaction. Customer privacy considerations, such as data encryption and destruction of records, ensure information is not stolen or abused.

subjective.question: List and explain the general tips to keep customers satisfied.
subjective.answer: Customers should always be treated courteously and with respect, especially under pressure, and helped willingly so they feel important, with their opinions given importance and preference. The employee's behaviour and personal appearance reflect on the company, since the employee is its emissary, so dressing well matters. Supplies of brochures, price lists and forms should be up to date, and calculators, phones and computers kept working, as these show how organised the employee is. The employee should continuously look for ways to help customers, never blame the company, an individual, the situation or conditions, always present the company positively, keep handy information about related products, and show enthusiasm without arrogance or personal moods.

subjective.question: How should customers with special needs be handled? Discuss children, the elderly, foreign visitors and disabled customers.
subjective.answer: Some customers cannot communicate or express their needs well, yet still need the product, so they need special handling. Children cannot explain things and need simple language, patient handling, nice words, something to play with, and special treatment rather than being ignored. The elderly need attention, honour and respect for their age; they explain things slowly, so the employee should listen patiently and not speak down to them. Foreign visitors face language problems and nervousness about local customs, so they should be listened to very carefully, spoken to slowly in easy language and short sentences, without shouting. Disabled and handicapped customers need top priority, should not be kept waiting, should be handled patiently with special aids, and should never be made to realise their handicap.

subjective.question: Why is good customer service important? Explain with reference to word of mouth, listening skills and rapport from the training workshop.
subjective.answer: Good customer service is important because it keeps customers coming back, generates good word-of-mouth advertising and does not cost much. Its financial impact is significant because a happy, repeat customer is valuable: a happy customer tells 4 others, while an unhappy customer tells 13 others. The workshop stresses discovering customer needs and developing listening skills. Effective listening means setting the stage by removing distractions, being open and accessible and listening with empathy; ensuring mutual understanding by reflecting feelings, paraphrasing main ideas and confirming next steps; listening to non-verbal signals; and suspending judgement. Building rapport depends on body language, voice control of speed, rhythm, tone, clarity and volume, and appropriate vocabulary.

subjective.question: Define strategic management and explain the three steps involved in strategy formulation.
subjective.answer: Strategic management is the process of specifying an organization's objectives, developing policies and plans to achieve these objectives, and allocating resources so as to implement the plans. It is the highest level of managerial activity, usually performed by the CEO and executive team, and provides overall direction to the whole enterprise. Strategy formulation involves, first, a situation analysis covering both internal and external factors and both micro-environmental and macro-environmental factors. Second, objectives are set, including vision statements, mission statements, overall corporate objectives, strategic business unit objectives, and tactical objectives. Third, these objectives, in the light of the situation analysis, suggest a strategic plan that provides the details of how to achieve them.

subjective.question: Describe the important measures required for successful strategy implementation.
subjective.answer: Successful implementation first requires allocation of sufficient resources, including financial resources, personnel, time, and technology support. Second, a chain of command or an alternative structure such as cross-functional teams must be established to remove ambiguity and confusion. Third, responsibility for specific tasks or processes must be assigned to specific individuals or groups, with clear job descriptions so that no one is unsure of their role. Fourth, the process itself must be managed: results are monitored, compared to benchmarks and best practices, efficacy and efficiency are evaluated, variances are controlled, and adjustments are made as necessary. Implementing specific programs also involves acquiring resources, developing the process, training, process testing, documentation, and integration with legacy processes.

subjective.question: Explain any five reasons why strategic plans fail.
subjective.answer: First, failure to understand the customer: knowing only statistical details is not enough, because different customers buy the same product for different reasons. Second, inability to predict environmental reaction, such as what competitors will do with fighting brands and price wars, or whether government will intervene. Third, over-estimation of resource competence, where staff, equipment, and processes cannot handle the new strategy and new skills are not developed. Fourth, failure to obtain employee commitment, because the new strategy is not well explained and no incentives are given. Fifth, poor communications, involving insufficient information sharing among stakeholders and exclusion of stakeholders and delegates. Any of these can stall or completely ruin an otherwise well-thought-out plan.

subjective.question: Discuss the specific skills required for successful CRM.
subjective.answer: CRM requires several specialized skills beyond general managerial skills. The skill to communicate is needed to explain CRM measures to staff and customers. The skill to listen means listening to understand, with patience, including what is not said. The skill to tolerate matters because a customer may be wrong, yet patience can win the deal. Managers also need the skill to foresee and anticipate developments, the skill to convince staff and customers through clear, logical argument, the skill to advise as a trusted expert, and the skill to educate staff and customers. Other skills include converting thinking, inducing action, minimizing FUD (fiasco, uncertainty, and doubt), creating desire, adding satisfaction, keeping promises, and anticipating difficulties.

subjective.question: What is customer retention? Why is it preferred, and what is its ultimate aim regarding types of customers?
subjective.answer: Customer retention is the process of keeping customers in the customer inventory for an unending period by meeting the needs and exceeding the expectations of those customers. It is preferred because it costs one tenth the cost of acquiring customers, builds a good image in the market, assures volume of sales so planning becomes easier, becomes a good reference in the market, and makes it easier to understand a customer over a long period. Customers enter as customers by chance, by occasion, by choice, or by repetition. The retention approach makes every effort to convert a customer by chance into a customer by loyalty, shifting the relationship from a mere transactional one to one tied up with emotion and commitment.

subjective.question: Explain the different types of customer loyalty.
subjective.answer: Customer loyalty may fall into several types. Loyalty towards brands arises from product characteristics or features that are somehow unique, such as taste, shape, size, longevity of use, or packing. Loyalty towards stores comes from customer handling and treatment, including extraordinary personal treatment regardless of the size of purchase. Loyalty towards organizations is mostly seen in service companies such as hotels, restaurants, and airlines, and is built on assurance of quality of service. Loyalty towards sales persons develops from total satisfaction with their services, confidence, pleasant manners, knowledge, helpful tendency, and advice. Finally, loyalty may be towards any other related aspect in the process of purchase and consumption that customers perceive as important.

subjective.question: How are customers classified according to loyalty, and what conversion should organizations aim for on the loyalty continuum?
subjective.answer: Customers may be classified under three heads. Hardcore loyalists maintain undivided loyalty regarding their brand choice; they restrict their choice to one or a selected few brands and normally would not switch brands. Soft-core loyalists divide their loyalty among a few available brands and select one or the other brand from among their choice of brands; having used a brand may itself be a reason for not selecting it in the immediate next purchase. The third group consists of switchers. On the loyalty continuum, organizations must focus their attention on converting switchers into soft-core loyalists and soft-core loyalists into hardcore loyal customers. How quickly this conversion is attained depends on the number of loyal customers in the organization's customer inventory.

subjective.question: Explain the process through which brand loyalty is attained.
subjective.answer: The process of attainment of brand loyalty starts with awareness of the fact that the brand is available, and creating such brand awareness is a major responsibility of the marketer. This requires developing a strong brand identity, which is a non-transferable means to establish the uniqueness of the brand in terms of its tangible and intangible attributes; its essence is what the brand stands for and how it differs from competitor brands. The identity must be repeatedly communicated to build familiarity, helped by a brand name that is simple, suggestive, memorable, unique, and meaningful. Brand recognition is the end result of brand familiarity. Positioning then frames a specific image, brand acceptance leads to brand selection, and satisfactory performance makes the customer insist on the same brand, finally becoming loyal.

subjective.question: Why do customers defect? Discuss the commonly found defection drivers.
subjective.answer: Customers defect for many reasons. They may move over to a different product category or shift to another type of product. They may be dissatisfied with the elements of the marketing mix, perceive better value for money from a competitor's offerings, or develop a misunderstanding with the value delivery system. A customer's specific need may not be fulfilled even though nothing is wrong with the product. Other drivers include displeasure at the point of purchase, dissatisfaction with after-sales service, an inherent feeling to try new products, compulsion due to technological and environmental forces, changing lifestyle and life-cycle stages, demographically moving away from the market place, communication evoking a poor response, and personal reasons, which can supersede all other reasons.

subjective.question: What strategies can an organization use to prevent customer defection and win back lapsed customers?
subjective.answer: Prevention begins with total knowledge about customer behavior, including behavior and migration patterns, supported by a transparent and interactive communication system. When signals of defection are noticed, special promotion campaigns should be launched. The organization should also develop barriers to exit: emotional appeal reminding the customer of a long relationship, conformance to specification and durability, lifetime utility, social relationship, flexibility, and added value. A customer-specific approach, concession price schemes, commitment, innovative approaches, and reducing risk also help. Organizations should establish a measurement system for satisfaction and defection rate, track losses regularly, form a customer care team focused on defection drivers, and introduce reward-based customer win-back programmes in which every win-back is celebrated and documented.
